heading: Climate and disease risk for livestock and fisheries
text:
Keywords: animal disease, mortality, heat stress, flood, drought, pond, fish kill, poultry disease, vaccination, veterinary access, insurance.
Pattern: animals and fish are exposed to disease outbreaks, heat stress, floods, drought and water-quality problems. A single outbreak or extreme weather event can wipe out a large share of the stock at once, and recovery takes a full production cycle.
Indicators: livestock, poultry or pond-based activity; distant veterinary or fisheries extension services; flood- or drought-prone site; no insurance.
Mitigation: insure the animals or stock where a scheme is available; follow a vaccination and biosecurity schedule; keep contact with the nearest veterinary or fisheries officer; do not stock beyond the water, shed and fodder capacity.

heading: Credit sales and delayed receivables
text:
Keywords: credit sales, payment delay, receivables, wholesaler, retailer, kirana credit, exporter payment, cooperative payment cycle, udhaar.
Pattern: buyers such as wholesalers, retailers, exporters, processors and cooperatives often pay after days or weeks, and small customers may buy on credit. Cash tied up in unpaid bills cannot pay for inputs or the loan instalment, even when the business is profitable on paper.
Indicators: sales to traders or institutions rather than cash customers; customary credit periods in the trade; no record of amounts owed.
Mitigation: keep a simple receivables register; set credit limits per customer; prefer UPI or cash on delivery for small buyers; keep working capital for at least one full payment cycle.

heading: Festival and peak-season concentration
text:
Keywords: festival season, wedding season, peak demand, seasonal sales, bridal bookings, school uniform season, idle months.
Pattern: a large part of annual sales happens in a few peak months (festivals, weddings, harvest, school reopening). Missing the peak because of late setup, stock shortages or supply delays loses much of the year's income, while fixed costs and instalments continue through quiet months.
Indicators: demand clearly higher in a few months; stock must be built before the peak; income in other months does not cover fixed costs.
Mitigation: time the launch and stock build-up ahead of the main season; save part of peak-season surplus for low months; add products or services that sell in the quiet months.

heading: Input price volatility
text:
Keywords: raw material price, feed cost, fodder, oilseed, grain price, commodity price swing, mandi price, harvest season, margin squeeze.
Pattern: the main raw material is an agricultural commodity or feed whose price moves with harvests, monsoon and mandi arrivals. When input prices rise faster than selling prices the operating margin can disappear for several months.
Indicators: one commodity makes up most of the variable cost; selling price is fixed by the local market or a buyer; no storage to buy inputs when they are cheap.
Mitigation: buy and store inputs after harvest when prices are lower, where storage is safe; join group purchasing with nearby units; grow part of the input (for example fodder) where possible; review selling prices when input costs change.

heading: Perishability and cold chain
text:
Keywords: perishable, spoilage, shelf life, milk, eggs, fish, fresh food, chilling, cold storage, transport delay, power cut.
Pattern: the product loses value within hours or days. Long or unreliable transport to the point of sale, power cuts that stop chilling, and days without buyers all turn directly into spoilage losses. Distance to the nearest market or collection point matters more than for durable goods.
Indicators: product sold fresh; no chilling or storage at the unit; point of sale more than a short trip away; road access that is disrupted in the monsoon.
Mitigation: schedule sales around fixed collection times; arrange access to a chilling centre or cold storage; keep a small backup power source for cooling; plan a value-added outlet (curd, ghee, dried or processed products) for unsold stock.

heading: Power reliability
text:
Keywords: electricity, three phase power, power cut, voltage fluctuation, motor, mill, machine downtime, generator, grid connection.
Pattern: machinery-based units (mills, expellers, pumps, sewing machines, chillers) cannot operate during outages or low voltage. Three-phase connections may not be available at the chosen site or may take time to sanction. Downtime reduces output and can damage motors.
Indicators: activity needs three-phase supply; site has only single-phase or irregular supply; no backup power budgeted.
Mitigation: confirm the connection type and supply hours at the exact site before buying machinery; budget for the connection application and wiring; plan working hours around supply schedules; consider a backup (generator, solar or inverter) where the process allows.

heading: Regulatory and licensing requirements
text:
Keywords: licence, permit, registration, FSSAI, NOC, panchayat, local body, trade licence, insurance, compliance delay.
Pattern: some activities need registrations, food safety licences, local body no-objection certificates or insurance before they can operate or sell to organised buyers. Delays in obtaining them postpone revenue while loan interest and fixed costs continue; operating without them risks closure or loss of buyers.
Indicators: food, animal or premises-related activity; buyers who ask for licence numbers; site in a residential area.
Mitigation: list every required licence before disbursement and apply early; include fees and waiting time in the launch plan; keep copies of approvals with the loan file.

heading: Single-buyer dependency
text:
Keywords: buyer concentration, one buyer, sole customer, exporter, master weaver, cooperative collection centre, contract dependence, bargaining power.
Pattern: most of the output is sold to one buyer or to a very small number of buyers (a single collection centre, one trader, one exporter or master weaver). If that buyer delays payment, cuts the price, changes quality requirements or stops buying, revenue can fall sharply with little notice, and the enterprise has weak bargaining power on price.
Indicators: fewer than three realistic sales channels; one buyer taking most of the volume; no written purchase terms; products made to one buyer's specification.

heading: Single-buyer dependency
text: Mitigation: develop at least two independent sales channels before scaling; keep direct local sales (households, haat, retail) as a fallback; agree written price and payment terms; avoid producing to a single buyer's specification without an advance or order.

heading: Working capital strain
text:
Keywords: working capital, cash flow gap, inventory, low season, instalment, moratorium end, stock build-up, liquidity.
Pattern: the unit needs cash for inputs, stock and wages before sales money arrives. Low-season months, credit sales and the end of the loan moratorium can create months where cash in is less than cash out, leading to missed instalments even for a viable business.
Indicators: several low-demand months; inputs bought in bulk; credit sales; instalments that start before sales stabilise.
Mitigation: keep a cash buffer covering at least one quarter's instalment; match the moratorium to the time needed to reach normal sales; avoid tying all working capital up in stock; track cash in and out monthly.

heading: Application process steps
text:
1. Confirm the business activity and the available margin money (your own contribution).
2. Check the scheme tier: the project cost decides whether the Micro Finance Scheme or the Term Loan Scheme applies.
3. Prepare a simple project report with the project cost, the capital expenditure and working capital split, and the repayment schedule.
4. Collect the required documents and self-attest the copies.
5. Complete the loan application form and submit it with the documents to the channelising agency or lending bank.
6. Attend verification: the agency checks the documents, may visit the business site and appraises the project report.
7. Receive the sanction letter stating the approved loan amount and terms.
8. Deposit or show proof of your margin contribution and sign the loan agreement.
9. Receive disbursement, usually paid directly to suppliers or into your bank account in stages.
10. Start repayment after the moratorium; keep receipts for every installment.

heading: After disbursement
text:
Use the loan only for the approved project. Keep records of purchases and sales. If repayment becomes
difficult, contact the agency before an installment is missed.

heading: Who the Micro Finance Scheme is for
text:
The Micro Finance Scheme is the smaller concessional tier. It serves very small income-generating
activities, such as a tailoring unit, a tea stall or a small backyard poultry unit, whose total project
cost does not exceed the Micro Finance ceiling. Eligibility and the loan amount are decided by fixed
rules in the financial engine, not by this document.

heading: Micro Finance Scheme key terms
text:
- Maximum project cost: ₹1,40,000
- Maximum loan amount: ₹1,25,000
- Beneficiary margin contribution: 10%
- Loan share of project cost: 90%
- Interest rate: 6.5% per annum
- Tenure: 3 years
- Moratorium: 3 months
- Repayment frequency: quarterly

heading: How the Micro Finance loan is repaid
text:
The loan is repaid over the tenure in quarterly installments. The moratorium is counted inside the
tenure: during the moratorium quarter only interest is paid and no principal. After the moratorium,
equal quarterly installments repay the principal with interest, and the final quarter clears the
remaining balance.

heading: Micro Finance loan cap
text:
The loan share is 90% of project cost, but the loan cannot exceed the maximum loan amount. For project
costs close to the ceiling, 90% of the cost is more than the cap, so the entrepreneur must contribute
slightly more than 10% to cover the difference.

heading: Who the Term Loan Scheme is for
text:
The Term Loan Scheme is the larger concessional tier. It serves income-generating projects whose total
project cost is above the Micro Finance ceiling of ₹1,40,000 and up to the Term Loan ceiling, such as a
dairy unit, a flour mill or a food processing unit. Projects costing more than the Term Loan ceiling are
outside the supported scheme range. Eligibility and the loan amount are decided by fixed rules in the
financial engine, not by this document.

heading: Term Loan Scheme key terms
text:
- Minimum project cost: above ₹1,40,000
- Maximum project cost: ₹50,00,000
- Maximum loan amount: ₹45,00,000
- Beneficiary margin contribution: 10%
- Loan share of project cost: 90%
- Interest rate: 8% per annum
- Tenure: 7 years
- Moratorium: 6 months
- Repayment frequency: quarterly

heading: How the Term Loan is repaid
text:
The loan is repaid over the tenure in quarterly installments. The moratorium is counted inside the
tenure: during the two moratorium quarters only interest is paid and no principal, giving the unit time
to start operating. After the moratorium, equal quarterly installments repay the principal with
interest, and the final quarter clears the remaining balance.

heading: How the Term Loan project cost is split
text:
The platform shows an indicative planning split of the project cost into 80% capital expenditure
(machinery, animals, shed, equipment) and 20% working capital (raw material, running costs until sales
begin). The lender's appraisal of the project report decides the actual split.
